roles.title: Foreign intelligence and assessment
roles.summary: Public country-of-origin reporting describes the ISI as having a foreign-intelligence role. This is a broad institutional description, not a disclosure of current collection methods, priorities or capabilities.

roles.title: Counter-intelligence
roles.summary: The EUAA’s June 2026 Country Focus describes counter-intelligence among the agency’s publicly reported functions. The public record does not establish the details of any internal unit or procedure.

roles.title: Domestic security and surveillance — reported
roles.summary: The EUAA’s October 2026 guidance reports surveillance concerns, including allegations concerning communications monitoring and links to repression. These are serious reported claims and are presented here as such, not as a complete or independently adjudicated account.

roles.title: Inter-service and inter-agency context
roles.summary: Older public country information describes intelligence coordination between the armed-services branches. Public descriptions vary by period and source; no current organisational chart is inferred here.

roles.title: Regional and bilateral intelligence relationships
roles.summary: Congressional research reports document U.S.–Pakistan intelligence cooperation related to Afghanistan during the 1980s and after 2001. Those accounts describe particular historical relationships, not the agency’s entire regional activity.

timeline.title: The ISI is established
timeline.summary: The EUAA’s June 2026 Country Focus states that the Inter-Services Intelligence Directorate was established in 1948. The available public sources used here do not provide enough primary documentation to reconstruct every detail of its founding arrangements.

timeline.title: War, separation and institutional reassessment
timeline.summary: The 1971 war and the separation of East Pakistan were major turning points in Pakistan’s national-security history. Later historical writing treats the period as an important test for the country’s military and intelligence institutions; this archive does not assign the outcome to a single agency.

timeline.title: U.S.–Pakistan intelligence cooperation in Afghanistan
timeline.summary: Congressional Research Service accounts describe American and Pakistani intelligence officers working together to train and supply Afghan resistance groups fighting Soviet forces, with U.S. assistance channelled through Pakistan’s ISI. The wider policy relationship also contained mistrust and competing interests.

timeline.title: A transformed U.S.–Pakistan security relationship
timeline.summary: After the attacks of 11 September 2001, Pakistan became a key partner in U.S.-led counterterrorism efforts. The 2009 CRS report describes cooperation alongside persistent questions about policy alignment and trust.

timeline.title: Questions about the ISI’s role enter sharper public debate
timeline.summary: The 2009 Congressional Research Service report records renewed U.S. scrutiny and competing assessments of the agency’s influence, autonomy and relationship with Pakistan’s military leadership. These are attributed policy assessments, not a definitive organisational finding.

cases.title: Afghanistan, the Cold War and intelligence cooperation
cases.summary: How public Congressional Research Service accounts describe the U.S.–Pakistan intelligence relationship during the Soviet-Afghan War — and why cooperation did not remove mutual mistrust.

body.p: The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979 reshaped regional security. During the 1980s, Afghan resistance groups fought Soviet forces and the Afghan government they supported. U.S. assistance to these groups was channelled through Pakistan’s Inter-Services Intelligence Directorate, according to Congressional Research Service histories.

CRS reporting describes American and Pakistani intelligence officers overseeing cooperative efforts to train and supply Afghan resistance groups. This supports a high-level account of bilateral cooperation; it does not provide a complete operational record, a full chain of command, or a reliable inventory of every recipient group.

The 2009 CRS report describes a relationship marked by both cooperation and mistrust. The same report records long-running U.S. questions about the ISI’s aims and role. The archive therefore avoids turning this history into a one-sided story of either seamless partnership or total disagreement.

This case study concerns publicly documented intelligence cooperation related to Afghanistan. It does not claim that every Afghan resistance activity, later militant movement or regional event was directed by the ISI.

cases.title: After 11 September: partnership and competing priorities
cases.summary: The post-9/11 realignment made Pakistan a key U.S. counterterrorism partner while leaving persistent policy disagreements in view.

body.p: The 11 September 2001 attacks and the subsequent U.S.-led campaign in Afghanistan transformed the U.S.–Pakistan relationship. The 2009 Congressional Research Service report describes Pakistan’s enlistment as a key ally in U.S.-led counterterrorism efforts.

The same report records praise for cooperation alongside doubts about the consistency of policy priorities. This is a useful reminder that intelligence partnerships are political relationships: shared objectives in one period or theatre do not prove agreement on every issue.

A general description of bilateral cooperation cannot establish the attribution of a specific operation, the identity of individual sources, or the precise role of a particular agency in an event. Such claims require their own reliable evidence.

cases.title: Institutional influence, oversight and public accountability
cases.summary: A reading guide to public assessments of intelligence influence, civilian oversight and allegations of rights violations — with careful separation of synthesis and adjudicated fact.

body.h: Why public accountability is difficult to assess
body.p: Intelligence institutions operate partly outside ordinary public visibility. As a result, public accounts often combine official statements, court records, journalism, academic analysis and human-rights reporting. These materials do not all carry the same evidentiary weight.

The EUAA’s October 2026 country guidance describes the ISI as a military-run body and summarises reports about communications monitoring and human-rights concerns. The page uses reporting language for these claims; it should not be read as a court judgment or a complete account of every alleged incident.

A claim is marked ‘Documented’ when supported by strong primary evidence or multiple credible sources; ‘Reported’ when credible attribution exists but the public primary record is incomplete; and ‘Disputed’ when credible accounts materially disagree. Allegations are not silently upgraded into established fact.

body.h: Questions the public record cannot settle
body.p: The source set used here cannot establish the full internal structure, current operational capabilities, classified directives, or every chain of responsibility. The archive leaves those questions open rather than filling them with speculation.

articles.title: How to read an intelligence history responsibly
articles.summary: A practical framework for separating public documentation, reporting, allegation and interpretation when the institution itself is partly opaque.

body.h: Start with the source, not the story
body.p: A dramatic claim can circulate for years without becoming better evidenced. Before repeating it, identify who made the claim, when it was published, what evidence was cited and whether another independent source confirms it.

body.h: Separate the event date from the publication date
body.p: A 2026 report can describe an event from decades earlier. Both dates matter. This archive records them separately so that a newly published summary is not mistaken for a new historical event.

‘The ISI did’ is a stronger statement than ‘a report attributed the activity to the ISI’. When attribution is indirect or contested, the writing should preserve that distinction in the sentence itself.

body.h: Treat silence as a limit, not an invitation
body.p: A missing public record does not prove that an event did or did not occur. It means the public record cannot establish it. The responsible response is to state the limit and avoid speculation.
Documented, Reported, Disputed and Unverified are editorial tools, not mathematical confidence scores. Each entry links to its supporting sources so readers can assess the evidence for themselves.

articles.title: An intelligence agency within a state security system
articles.summary: A high-level introduction to public descriptions of the ISI, its military context and the limits of what open sources can show.

body.h: An institution with a partial public record
body.p: The Inter-Services Intelligence Directorate is widely described in public sources as Pakistan’s principal intelligence agency. The EUAA’s October 2026 country guidance describes it as a military-run body led by a three-star army general. Such descriptions provide context; they are not a substitute for a complete public legal or organisational record.

The EUAA’s June 2026 Pakistan Country Focus states that the ISI was established in 1948. A more detailed history requires specialist scholarship and careful comparison of accounts, including the historical monograph by Hein G. Kiessling.

Recent EUAA country information describes foreign intelligence, counter-intelligence and domestic-security dimensions. These labels should remain broad. Public summaries cannot establish classified methods, internal reporting lines or current tasking.

The agency’s place in the wider security system has been debated by researchers and policymakers. That debate includes questions about military influence, civilian oversight and allegations of rights violations. A responsible history must include these debates without treating every allegation as proven.

articles.title: The 1980s relationship: cooperation without certainty
articles.summary: What Congressional Research Service accounts say about U.S.–Pakistan intelligence cooperation during the Soviet-Afghan War.

body.p: The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979 created a new arena of strategic competition. Through the 1980s, the United States supported Afghan resistance groups, with assistance channelled through Pakistan’s ISI, according to public Congressional Research Service histories.

The 2009 CRS report describes close U.S. links with Pakistan’s ISI dating to the 1980s and identifies cooperative efforts to train and supply Afghan resistance fighters. A separate CRS Afghanistan report also describes U.S. assistance through the ISI.

The existence of cooperation does not mean the partners shared every objective. CRS accounts also describe mistrust and disagreement. The public historical record is better understood as a relationship shaped by overlapping interests, unequal information and competing priorities.
